text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementZoologyHow Jumping Spiders SleepRemarkably like us with cycles of wakefulness and REMDRBy Devin Reese11:00 AM CDT on October 27, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleMyriad studies focus on human sleep, from mapping circadian rhythms to determining optimal sleep length. But we’re not the only creatures that need some shut-eye. The same is also true even of invertebrates, though far less is known about their sleep patterns. Which is why a new study published yesterday in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences decided to take a closer look at spider sleep in particular. Powered By 10 ShareNextStayIt’s obviously tough to conduct an electroencephalogram on a spider the length of a rice grain. And so, led by biologists in Germany, with colleagues from Australia and Italy, the study took a new approach to examining the sleep behavior of Australian jumping spiders (Portia fimbriata). Such arachnids are typically active in the daytime, then asleep at night in characteristic legs-pulled-in postures that camouflage them against foliage or rocks.Read more: “Why Do Spiders Decorate Their Webs?
